Use Supabase as your comprehensive backend solution.

## Introduction

::: {.callout}
Nostalgic for the websites of the last millennium, I used Supabase to build a retro-inspired [guestbook application](/samples/content-engineering/personal/guestbook/) with some modern touches: anti-spam measures, an admin dashboard gated by Google OAuth 2.0, and email notifications powered by Gmail API.

<!-- ::: {.iframe url="https://y2k-guestbook.vercel.app/" title="y2k Guestbook" zoom="50%"} -->
<!-- ::: -->

:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Install Your Own**:

[{{< fa brands github >}} beck-chan/y2k-guestbook](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook){target="_blank" .button}

:::

Building a web application is a lot of moving pieces. After all, what the user interacts with is just the surface of the iceberg, so to speak. 

Maybe admitting this next bit will brand me as an imposter, but I have to be honest and say that while I'm fairly comfortable with digging around in the frontend, I've always felt a tad intimidated by backend infrastructure. Some of the reason being that traditionally, those moving pieces were generally discrete, meaning that you had juggle a lot of different tools and services without a unified platform to help you manage them.

Enter **[Supabase](https://supabase.com/){target="_blank"}**: A comprehensive backend-as-a-service platform that provides a suite of tools to help you connect everything and oversee all the moving pieces — from your database tables, to ready-made ways to read and write those tables, to user authentication, to functions that perform tasks when a row changes, and more. 

So incredibly user-friendly, that a self-professed backend novice like myself managed to cobble together a solution for my Next.js application that does exactly what I wanted it to do.

## From browser to backend

The usual way to read and write a database from a website is to build a small server of your own, whose only job is to answer web requests and talk to the database for you. Since the program can only answer requests while it's turned on, on a computer the internet can reach, you have to have a reliable way to keep that program running. You can keep a physical machine plugged in and connected to the internet, or hand the program to a hosting service that keeps a copy running for you.

For example, our guestbook needs functionality to:

- **Retrieve comments:** Show a public version of comments that have been submitted.
- **Save comments:** Store comments after checks have passed for length, content, and frequency.
- **Modify comments:** Let administrators edit, delete, or mark a comment read.
- **Apply settings:** Adjust guestbook settings, such as allowed comment length and frequency limits.

So you invent one web address for "get the comments," another for "save a comment," and so on. Each address is an instruction in that program — when a request shows up, run this database query and send the result back. 

You also have to protect each instruction, since not everyone should be able to perform all actions. For example, the address that saves a comment must not let a stranger delete comments. Every interaction with the database needs its own address in that program, and its own check to make sure the person asking is allowed to do that. The program that holds all of those addresses is the server you keep running.

### Supabase Data REST API

::: {.callout}
The Supabase [Data REST API](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/api/rest/overview){target="_blank"} "auto-generates an API directly from your database schema allowing you to connect to your database through a restful interface, directly from the browser."

:::

Supabase eliminates the need to build and run a separate server just to read and write the database. Instead, you can connect directly to the database from your website using the Data REST API. Instead of inventing an address for each action, you name the table, and Supabase turns that name into the address. 

Instead of putting a separate check on each address, Supabase enforces the check on the table itself using [Row Level Security](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security){target="_blank"}. Each request carries a token that says who is calling and what they are allowed to do, for example:

- Visitors have access to read public comments and submit comments without needing to sign in, authenticated with Supabase's [publishable key](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/api-keys#which-key-do-you-use){target="_blank"}.
- Approved administrators have access to manage comments and settings after they sign in. That sign-in carries a note — [when the note says `admin`](#auth), the database runs a check called `is_admin()` and allows the change.

The API URL is your "RESTful endpoint for querying and managing your database." For example, `https://<your-project>.supabase.co/rest/v1/` is the front door to your tables. In our guestbook, a helper called `createClient()` in [`src/lib/supabase/server.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/src/lib/supabase/server.ts){target="_blank"} opens that door:

```typescript
return createServerClient(
  // Your Supabase project URL
  process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
  // Your Supabase publishable key
  process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY!,
  // ...
);
```

Under the hood, asking for a table becomes a normal web request to `https://<your-project>.supabase.co/rest/v1/<table>`:

::: {.panel-tabset}

# Retrieve comments

`comments_public` is a table with a view of submitted `comments` that exclude submitted email addresses from display. The `getPublicCommentsPage` function reads that table in [`src/app/actions/comments.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/src/app/actions/comments.ts){target="_blank"}:

```typescript
supabase
  .from("comments_public")
  .select("id, display_name, body, created_at, updated_at", { count: "exact" })
  .order("created_at", { ascending: false })
```

# Save comments

`comments` is the private table that stores submitted comments. The `submitComment` function in [`src/app/actions/comments.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/src/app/actions/comments.ts){target="_blank"} writes to this table.

Comments are first checked for length, content, and frequency:

```typescript
const lengthError = commentLengthError(
  name,
  email,
  body,
  settings.commentLength,
);
if (lengthError) {
  return { ok: false, error: lengthError };
}

const hit = checkCommentProfanity(name, body, settings.profanityAllowList);
const profanityError = profanityErrorMessage(hit);
if (profanityError) {
  return { ok: false, error: profanityError };
}

const limited = await consumeCommentRateLimit(await clientIp(), settings);
if (!limited.ok) {
  return limited;
}
```

Only if all checks pass, then the comment is written to the `comments` table:

```typescript
const supabase = await createClient();
const { error } = await supabase.from("comments").insert({
  display_name: name,
  email: email || null,
  body,
});
```

# Modify comments

The `loadAdminComments` function in in [`src/app/actions/comments.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/src/app/actions/comments.ts){target="_blank"} reads the private `comments` table for the dashboard:

```typescript
supabase
  .from("comments")
  // Display the email address to administrators
  .select("id, display_name, email, body, is_read, created_at, updated_at")
  .order("created_at", { ascending: false })
```

The `updateComment`, `deleteComment`, `setCommentRead`, and `setCommentsRead` functions allow administrators to edit and delete comments, as well as toggle comment read status:

```typescript
// updateComment
supabase
  .from("comments")
  .update({
    display_name: name,
    email: email || null,
    body,
  })
  .eq("id", input.id)

// deleteComment
supabase.from("comments").delete().eq("id", id)

// setCommentRead
supabase.from("comments").update({ is_read: read }).eq("id", id)

// setCommentsRead
supabase.from("comments").update({ is_read: read }).in("id", uniqueIds)
```

Permission to modify comments is enforced by row-level security rules, that we set when we created the `comments` table with our [schema.sql](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/schema.sql){target="_blank"}:

```sql
create policy "admin_update_comments"
  on public.comments
  for update
  to authenticated
  using (public.is_admin())
  with check (public.is_admin());

create policy "admin_delete_comments"
  on public.comments
  for delete
  to authenticated
  using (public.is_admin());
```

Both policies call the `is_admin()` function defined in [`src/app/actions/auth.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/src/app/actions/auth.ts){target="_blank"}:

```typescript
export async function isAdmin() {
  const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.getUser();
  return data.user?.app_metadata.role === "admin";
}
```

Which checks whether or not the user is an authorized admin:

```sql
select coalesce(
  (auth.jwt() -> 'app_metadata' ->> 'role') = 'admin',
  false
);
```

# Apply settings

The `guestbook_settings` table is one record with the comment length, the speed limit, and how many notes fit on a page. The `loadGuestbookSettings` function in [`src/lib/loadGuestbookSettings.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/src/lib/loadGuestbookSettings.ts){target="_blank"} reads these saved settings:

```typescript
supabase
  .from("guestbook_settings")
  .select("*")
  .eq("id", 1)
  .maybeSingle()
```

`saveGuestbookSettings` in [`src/app/actions/settings.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/src/app/actions/settings.ts){target="_blank"} allows administrators to adjust these settings, first checking that the user is an admin:

```typescript
const { supabase, error: authError } = await requireAdmin();
if (!supabase) {
  return { ok: false, error: authError };
}
```

Only if that check passes, then the settings row is edited:

```typescript
supabase.from("guestbook_settings").update(row).eq("id", 1)
```

:::

## Authentication gating by Google

<!-- DO NOT EDIT ABOVE HERE -->

The usual way to add "Sign in with Google" is to run your own login service. You register the app with Google, store users in a table you maintain, hand the browser a cookie that says they are signed in, and remember to check that cookie on every private page. Miss one check and a stranger can open the dashboard.

Supabase Auth holds that Google conversation and the signed-in session. A session is the site remembering that this browser already signed in. Signing in still only says who the person is. `admin_allowlist` is the short list of admin email addresses.

After Google sends the person back to `/admin/login`, `ensure_admin_role` in [`scripts/schema.sql`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/scripts/schema.sql){target="_blank"} looks up their address. If it is not on the list, the function returns false:

```sql
if user_email is null
   or not exists (
     select 1 from public.admin_allowlist where email = user_email
   ) then
  return false;
end if;
```

Only if the address is on the list, then it writes `app_metadata.role` set to `admin`. That note sits where the visitor cannot edit it:

```sql
update auth.users
set raw_app_meta_data =
  coalesce(raw_app_meta_data, '{}'::jsonb) || '{"role":"admin"}'::jsonb
where id = uid
  and coalesce(raw_app_meta_data->>'role', '') is distinct from 'admin';
```

When the account is first created, `hook_before_user_created` in the same file reads that list. If the address is missing, sign-up is refused:

```sql
if user_email is null
   or user_email = ''
   or not exists (
     select 1 from public.admin_allowlist where email = user_email
   ) then
  return jsonb_build_object(
    'error',
    jsonb_build_object(
      'message', 'Not authorized',
      'http_code', 403
    )
  );
end if;
```

Only if the address is on the list, then the same role is written onto the new login:

```sql
return jsonb_build_object(
  'user',
  jsonb_build_object(
    'app_metadata',
    jsonb_build_object('role', 'admin')
  )
);
```

`is_admin()` trusts only that note. The `proxy` function in [`src/proxy.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/src/proxy.ts){target="_blank"} runs the check on admin pages. Everyone else can sign the book with no account at all.

The role on the session is read first:

```typescript
const role =
  user && typeof user.app_metadata?.role === "string"
    ? user.app_metadata.role
    : null;
const isAdmin = role === "admin";
```

If there is no session yet, they are sent to `/admin/login`. If the note does not say admin, they are signed out and sent home with `?admin_error=1`. If they are already signed in as an admin, they go straight to the dashboard:

```typescript
if (!user) {
  const loginUrl = request.nextUrl.clone();
  loginUrl.pathname = loginPath;
  loginUrl.search = "";
  return redirectWithCookies(loginUrl, supabaseResponse);
}

if (!isAdmin) {
  await supabase.auth.signOut();
  const homeUrl = request.nextUrl.clone();
  homeUrl.pathname = guestbookHomePath();
  homeUrl.search = "admin_error=1";
  return redirectWithCookies(homeUrl, supabaseResponse);
}

if (isLogin) {
  const adminUrl = request.nextUrl.clone();
  adminUrl.pathname = adminPath;
  adminUrl.search = "";
  return redirectWithCookies(adminUrl, supabaseResponse);
}
```

If the dashboard moves off `/admin`, the same check follows whatever path is in `NEXT_PUBLIC_GUESTBOOK_ADMIN_PATH`. The Google setup steps are in [Prerequisites](https://beck-chan.vercel.app/docs/prerequisites){target="_blank"}.

`admin_allowlist` is the list the browser is not supposed to see. The `loadAllowlist` function in [`supabase/functions/_shared/allowlist.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/supabase/functions/_shared/allowlist.ts){target="_blank"} reads it with a server key:

```typescript
const url = Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_URL");
const key = Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY");

const supabase = createClient(url, key, {
  auth: { persistSession: false, autoRefreshToken: false },
});
const { data, error } = await supabase.from("admin_allowlist").select("email");
```

## Edge Functions mail on a write

The usual way to email yourself when a comment arrives is to run a second program next to the site. It watches the database, or you put new comments on a queue and a worker reads that queue, and you have to keep that worker awake overnight.

Supabase runs a small program in the cloud when a row changes. They call these Edge Functions. The database calls the function with a webhook, and the function sends the email. `FLAG_NOTIF` is the on/off switch. When it is off, the functions stay where they are and send nothing.

`notify-admins` in [`supabase/functions/notify-admins/index.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/supabase/functions/notify-admins/index.ts){target="_blank"} covers changes to comments, settings, and the admin list. It ignores the call unless the request carries `NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, and it stays quiet unless `FLAG_NOTIF` is on:

```typescript
if (!verifyNotifySecret(req)) {
  return jsonResponse(401, { error: "Unauthorized" });
}
if (!flagNotifOn()) {
  return jsonResponse(200, { skipped: "FLAG_NOTIF" });
}
```

`verifyNotifySecret` in [`supabase/functions/_shared/env.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/supabase/functions/_shared/env.ts){target="_blank"} compares the request with that shared password:

```typescript
const expected = Deno.env.get("NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_SECRET") ?? "";
if (!expected) return false;
const auth = req.headers.get("authorization") ?? "";
const header = req.headers.get("x-notify-webhook-secret") ?? "";
const bearer = auth.match(/^Bearer\s+(.+)$/i)?.[1]?.trim() ?? "";
return header === expected || bearer === expected || auth === expected;
```

The people who receive the mail are the addresses from `loadAllowlist()`. A new comment fills the `comment-insert` template and sends it with the Gmail API:

```typescript
const copy = await loadMail("comment-insert", { admin, name, body });
return allowlist.map((to) => ({
  to,
  ...copy,
  idempotencyKey: `comment:insert:${id}:${to}`,
}));
```

An edit sends mail only when the name, the email, or the text changed. A timestamp change does not:

```typescript
const keys = ["display_name", "email", "body"] as const;
return keys.some((key) => str(oldRecord?.[key]) !== str(record?.[key]));
```

`on-user-created` in [`supabase/functions/on-user-created/index.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/supabase/functions/on-user-created/index.ts){target="_blank"} covers a brand-new account. It uses those same two checks, then fills the `auth-created` template for the allowlist.

How this is turned on is in [Enable Notifications](https://beck-chan.vercel.app/docs/notifs){target="_blank"}.

## Rate limits live in Postgres

Leave a comment box wide open and a script can fill the board in a minute. The usual fix is a separate counter store, often Redis, or the memory of whichever copy of the site happened to answer. Restart the site and the count forgets everyone. Two copies of the site can disagree about whether this person already posted.

The counters live in the Postgres database Supabase already hosts, so a restart does not wipe them and every copy of the site sees the same number. By default a visitor can leave one comment every five minutes, and two in a day. Those numbers can be raised in the guestbook settings.

`submitComment` spends one of those chances by calling `consumeCommentRateLimit` in [`src/lib/rate-limit.ts`](https://github.com/beck-chan/y2k-guestbook/blob/main/src/lib/rate-limit.ts){target="_blank"}. The function does not store the visitor's raw internet address. It stores a scrambled version of it:

```typescript
function hashIp(ip: string) {
  return createHash("sha256").update(ip).digest("hex").slice(0, 32);
}

const key = hashIp(ip || "unknown");
```

The counting tool is `rate-limiter-flexible`. It writes the counters to `guestbook_rate_limits`. The browser cannot write that table. Only the server can:

```typescript
new RateLimiterPostgres({
  storeClient,
  storeType: "pool",
  points: opts.points,
  duration: opts.duration,
  keyPrefix: opts.keyPrefix,
  tableName: "guestbook_rate_limits",
  tableCreated: tableReady,
})
```

Only if both the short window and the daily window still have room, then the function spends one chance in each:

```typescript
await daily.consume(key);
await burst.consume(key);
```

The docs chatbot counts questions the same way, in a table called `docs_chat_limits`: five an hour, and ten a day, again from a scrambled internet address. Every question costs a call to Gemini, the model that writes the reply.

## pgvector searches the docs

The docs are long, and searching for the exact words someone typed misses questions asked a different way. The usual fix is a second search engine. You copy the docs into it and keep that copy in step with the real pages, or the answers drift.

Supabase keeps that search in the same Postgres database. `pgvector` stores a list of numbers standing in for the meaning of a chunk of text. Those numbers are called an embedding. Gemini creates them, and they are kept in `docs_section`, next to the words they came from.

When someone asks the chatbot a question, that question becomes the same kind of list of numbers. Postgres looks for the chunks whose numbers are close, and it also does an ordinary word search. The chat keeps the few pages that do well on either test, and Gemini may only answer from those excerpts. The reply includes links back to those pages.

On the public version of the site, only pages marked public are searched. The visitor's browser never reads `docs_section` directly. The chat page on the server does, with a key that stays on the server. The build notes are in the [chatbot build](https://beck-chan.vercel.app/docs/bot-build){target="_blank"}.

Those same tables are the catalog in [Build API documentation with Scalar](../api/index.qmd). The comment path, speed limit included, is what [Automate tests with Cucumber and Playwright](../cucumber/index.qmd) checks. The number on the page is [Implement hit counters with PostHog](../posthog/index.qmd).
